# From Metrics to Practice: Rethinking and Refining the AI Literacy Scale for Teachers

**Yimin Ning1,2** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-6491-0906) **E. Anni2 · Dengming Yao1 · Binyan Xu1,3 · Tommy Tanu Wijaya4**

Received: 29 October 2024 / Revised: 10 March 2026 / Accepted: 17 July 2026 © De La Salle University 2026

# Abstract This study develops a teacher AI literacy scale comprising six dimensions: perception of AI, AI knowledge, AI skills, applications of AI, innovation of AI, and AI ethics. The research involved three sequential phases. In the first phase, a Random Forest Model (RFM) was employed to select 30 representative items from an initial pool of 60 questions. The second phase focused on psychometric validation using the Rasch model. Results demonstrated that the overall scale met psychometric standards, with all item fit indices falling within acceptable ranges. In the third phase, the validated scale was applied to a sample of 658 teachers using Latent Class Analysis (LCA). The analysis revealed five distinct latent classes of AI literacy among teachers: AI Pioneers, Practical Teachers, Developing Teachers, Emerging AI Teachers, and Tradi- tional Teachers. In sum, the scale is promising but still requires cross-cultural validation and predictive-validity checks.

## Highlights

- The Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale for Teachers (AILST) assesses teachers’ AI literacy across six dimensions: perception of AI, AI knowledge, AI skills, applications of AI, innovation of AI, and AI ethics.
- AILST was developed and validated through a three-phase process involving random forest modeling, Rasch analysis, and latent class analysis, with strong psychometric results.
- Latent class analysis identified five teacher profiles: AI Pioneers, Practical Teachers, Developing Teachers, Emerging AI Teachers, and Traditional Teachers, enabling differentiated training and targeted policy support.

**Keywords** Teachers · Artificial intelligence · Literacy · AIED

**Table 4** Item fit and error statistics for the scale

and the data were highly reliable. The correlation between each item and the overall test construct was also calculated. Higher correlation coefficients indicate stronger alignment between an item and the intended measurement goal (Tran- tham et al., 2022). In this study, the item-total correlations ranged from 0.47 to 0.78, all of which were positively corre- lated with the overall construct, further supporting the con- struct validity of the scale. Item fit was assessed using Infit Mean Square (Infit MNSQ) and Outfit Mean Square (Outfit MNSQ) statistics. The acceptable range for both indices is typically set between 0.5 and 1.5 (Lombaerts et al., 2009). The Outfit MNSQ values ranged from 0.47 to 1.45, while the Infit MNSQ values ranged from 0.58 to 1.47—all falling within the acceptable range, indicating a good fit between the items and the Rasch model. Additionally, Z-standard- ized fit statistics (Infit ZSTD and Outfit ZSTD) were used to evaluate the statistical significance of misfit. Ideal values are close to 0, and values between − 2 and + 2 are considered indicative of adequate fit. In this study, all items demon- strated Infit and Outfit ZSTD values within the − 2 to + 2 

range, confirming the appropriateness of item fit (Antoni- etti et al., [2023)](#appendix-ai-literacy-scale-for-teachers-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-bowen-fang-for). Overall, these results demonstrate that the items in the scale exhibit good psychometric quality and fit the Rasch model well. This supports the use of the scale for accurately assessing teachers’ AI literacy levels. In the Rasch model, both person ability and item dif- ficulty are converted into an equal-interval scale using a logarithmic transformation, referred to as logit units (van de Grift et al., 2014). These distributions are visually rep- resented through the Wright Map (see Fig. [2)](#application-of-scale). The vertical line in the center of the figure represents the logit scale, with “M” indicating the mean, “S” representing one standard deviation, and “T” representing two standard deviations (Yan & Pastore, 2022). On the left side of the scale, the logit values correspond to the distribution of teachers' AI liter- acy levels. Higher positions indicate greater ability, while lower positions reflect reduced ability. The distribution uses symbols to represent frequency: each “#” represents three teachers, and each “.” represents one or two teachers (Kos- chmieder & Neubauer, 2021). On the right side of the scale, 

1. Ning et al.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

 the numbered items correspond to item difficulty, arranged from most to least difficult from top to bottom. As shown in Fig. [2,](#application-of-scale) the range of teacher ability spans approximately 6 logit units, whereas item difficulty spans about 15 logit units. Ideally, in a well-balanced Wright Map, the distribu- tion of item difficulties should correspond to the distribution of person abilities. That is, areas with higher concentrations of participants should be matched with a greater number of items at similar difficulty levels, and high-ability teachers should be matched with appropriately challenging items. In this study, both person ability and item difficulty are con- centrated in the middle of the logit scale, suggesting that teacher ability is approximately normally distributed. More- over, the mean ability (M) of the participants is close to the mean item difficulty, indicating that the overall difficulty level of the items was appropriate. However, the distribu- tion also reveals a shortage of high-difficulty items that cor- respond to high-ability teachers, indicating that the upper end of the ability spectrum is not fully covered by the exist- ing item set.

### Application of Scale

LCA is a statistical method used to classify individuals and identify group heterogeneity based on their differ- ing response patterns to categorical indicator variables. To determine the optimal number of scale types, five models were fitted in this study, with the number of classes rang- ing from _k_ = 2 to _k_ = 6. Fit indices improved from the 2- to 5-class models, and the LMR-LRT/BLRT supported the 5-class solution over the 4-class model (_p_ \< .05), whereas the 6-class model did not yield significant improvement (LMR _p_ \> .05). The 5-class model achieved high classifi- cation quality (entropy = 0.984; AvePP ≥ .80) and adequate class sizes (smallest class ≥ 9.7%), indicating stable and reli- able profiles. When _k_ = 5, the entropy reached its maximum value of 0.984, indicating that the model with five latent classes exhibited high classification accuracy. Therefore, the model with five latent classes was ultimately selected. According to the overall chi-square test results presented in Tables [5 ](#application-of-scale)and 6, significant differences were observed across Groups 1 through 5.
